Female skilfish (Erilepis zonifer) attain an ultimate total length of 188 centimeters [Li = 188 centimeters], placing them among the largest of the hexagrammoid fishes. This substantial body size is consistent with the species’ life in deep, cold waters of the North Pacific, where it occupies a high trophic position as a piscivorous predator. The total length at which females first reach puberty is 83 centimeters [Lp = 83 centimeters], a value that indicates a prolonged juvenile phase before reproductive maturation commences. The interval from the hatching of the pelagic egg to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva, occurring at a stable water temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], is approximately 49 days [ab = approximately 49 days]. This protracted developmental period at such a low thermal regime likely reflects the slow metabolic pace typical of cold-water and deep-sea fishes. The yolk-sac larva itself initially relies entirely on the endogenous yolk reserves, and the entire incubation process under these conditions demands a steady thermal environment, which is typical for this species’ reproductive grounds. The prolonged duration of embryonic development at 4.1 °C, among the coldest thermal regimes tolerated by any teleost of comparable body size, underscores the species' adaptation to a high-latitude environment. This extended developmental phase also has implications for the timing of the reproductive season, as females must commit to egg deposition well in advance of the seasonal availability of their larval prey.

The wet weight at birth for skilfish is approximately 4.2 milligrams [Wwb = approximately 4.2 milligrams], based on an egg diameter comparable to that of the closely related sablefish (Anoplopoma fimbria). This small initial body mass gradually increases as the larva transitions to exogenous feeding, during which it begins to capture small zooplanktonic prey. The juvenile to sub-adult phase is accompanied by a considerable acceleration in mass gain. Once females approach sexual maturation, their body composition undergoes marked changes in preparation for reproduction. The age at which individuals reach the end of their natural lifespan, again at a constant ambient temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], has been estimated at approximately 80 years [am = approximately 80 years]. This extreme longevity is among the highest recorded for any scorpaeniform fish and is consistent with the slow life-history strategy that characterizes many deep-water species. The combination of a minute starting mass and a decadal growth trajectory illustrates how the species achieves its impressive final size through a sustained, low-metabolic investment over many years.

At the onset of puberty, which occurs when females have attained a total length of 83 centimeters [Lp = 83 centimeters], the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 7.6 kilograms [Wwp = 7.6 kilograms]. This represents a substantial increase from the initial size at birth, reflecting many years of somatic growth. The size at first reproduction is closely tied to the species’ ability to secure sufficient energy reserves to support a reproductive event. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown female, reached at the asymptotic length of 188 centimeters [Li = 188 centimeters], is approximately 88.5 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 88.5 kilograms]. This enormous body mass is consistent with the species’ role as a large apex predator, comparable in mass to other large-bodied deep-water fishes such as the lingcod. Achieving such a final size requires a very slow growth rate that extends across many decades. The allometric relationship linking length to mass in this species suggests that females invest disproportionately in skeletal growth during early life before shifting resources toward mass accretion later on.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their deep-water habitat (4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]), the annual reproductive output of mature female skilfish is notable for its combination of high fecundity and a slow schedule. This modest reproductive frequency is characteristic of many long-lived, late-maturing marine teleosts that invest heavily in a small number of large, slow-developing eggs. The trade-off between clutch size and egg size reflects the cold-water constraints on larval development, where larger eggs provide greater yolk reserves that enhance survival during the prolonged incubation phase.

The maximum longevity of 80 years [am = 80 years] places skilfish among the most long-lived of known teleosts, a life span that necessitates late maturation and a very low natural mortality rate at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. For a female, the age at first successful spawning is estimated to follow shortly after puberty, but the precise interval between reaching the length of 83 centimeters [Lp = 83 centimeters] and the first spawning event can vary considerably. The age at birth, defined as the time from egg fertilization to eclosion of the yolk-sac larva, is 49 days [ab = 49 days] at 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], which is a prolonged incubation period compared to warmer-water congeners. The overall life history is thus one of extreme investment in individual survival and slow turnover, with the ultimate length of 188 centimeters [Li = 188 centimeters] representing the culmination of a very slow but steady growth trajectory. This strategy makes the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation due to its low intrinsic rate of population increase. The extreme longevity of eight decades places this species in a demographic category with other deep-water teleosts, such as the orange roughy and certain groupers, all of which share a low replacement rate that requires decades to recover from population declines.
